We have carbon NMR peaks: 169.52, 132.43,130.27,129.30,126.70,126.66,123.57,43.30,26.29 ppm.

Methyl carbons typically around 10-30 ppm. Here we have peaks at 43.30 and 26.29. 43 ppm could be a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl adjacent, or a CH3 attached to N or O). 26.29 is typical for aliphatic CH2/CH3. Need to determine number of methyl groups. Methyl carbon appears as a single carbon per CH3. So count peaks that correspond to methyl carbons. Possibly two methyl groups: one at 26.29 (alkyl CH3) and one at 43.30 (maybe a carbonyl-adjacent CH3, like acetyl CH3). The other peaks are aromatic/sp2 and carbonyl (169.52). So likely 2 methyl groups.

But need to be sure: Could 43.30 be a quaternary carbon? Quaternary sp3 carbon attached to carbonyl maybe around 45 ppm. But methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) appears ~30 ppm. 43 is a bit high but could be a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., O-CH3). O-methyl appears ~55 ppm. So 43 maybe a CH2? But CH2 typical 20-40. So maybe it's a CH2 not methyl. However we have only one low-field aliphatic carbon at 26.29, which is likely a methyl. So maybe only 1 methyl.

We need more info: Could use proton NMR to see number of methyl signals. Let's get proton NMR.
